title: Auk’s egg, prize of their fray
html_source:
The great auk was a flightless bird of the alcid family that became extinct in the mid-19th century. It was the only modern species in the genus Pinguinus. The eggs, unusual looking, white, mottled with black marmoreal markings featured a rather unique pointed oval shape. They became an expensive and prized acquisition for ornithologists and other collectors, which prior to the bird’s extinction, contributed to the population’s demise. The bird was flightless and awkward which compounded its vulnerability. Joyce frequently references birds throughout this book, in particular in reference to Stephen. Towards the end of the chapter, Stephen refers to himself as a hawklike man and speaks of his lapwing.

The reference to the auk’s egg here might have a double signification. Firstly this could refer on a visual level to the shape of Stephen’s head. However more importantly, like the auk, Stephen is a rare creature. The sentence, the use of the word ‘meek’ suggests he may, like the bird, be somewhat ungainly, sensitive and susceptible to the other’s who surround him. For example, we get the feeling Buck Mulligan bullies him around somewhat. Yet his intellectual brilliance is unusual and makes him a rare oddity, like the auk, his thoughts, like the eggs of the auk, are prized. His genius is coveted by the others who in their verbal disputes seek to win him over or sway him to their arguments. I cannot help feeling that Stephen represents a young Joyce, an unusually erudite and intelligent young man whose rare brilliance makes him at once overly sensitive yet also makes others crave his company or approval.
